message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Van name ideas for the staff vote

- **The Restoration Wagon**
- **Old Faithful**
- **Chippendale Express**
- **The Dovetail**
- **Varnish Van**

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

Some fixed points decide the order:
- **C has to be last.** The office won't accept anything before 11:00.
- **A can't come before B.** Even leaving at 08:30, the driver reaches A at 09:00, finishes at 09:15, and reaches B at 09:40, after the shop has opened.

So the order is **B, then A, then C**.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave the depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B** (20 min drive) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B. Done before the 09:30 opening ✓ |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive B → A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A, within the 09:00–10:00 window ✓ |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive A → C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break** near C, while waiting for 11:00 |
| 10:55–11:00 | Spare 5 minutes |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at **C**, from 11:00 ✓ |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive C → depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at the depot** ✓ |

**This plan has no spare time at the end.** C can't start before 11:00, unloading takes 15 minutes and the drive back takes 45, so the van gets back at exactly 12:00 whatever order you choose. Any delay at C, such as a slow handover, a parking problem or traffic, makes him late.

Before tomorrow, either:
- ask the office whether they could accept at 10:45 or 10:50, or
- check whether the 12:00 return is firm, and tell whoever needs the van that it may be a few minutes late.

## "Driver arriving" text, friendlier version

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Business]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three things to check before handing furniture over

1. **Condition:** look the piece over with the customer for scratches, dents or marks from the journey, so any issue is noted on the spot.
2. **Completeness:** confirm it's the right item and nothing is missing, such as keys, shelves, handles, glass panels or fixings.
3. **Function and placement:** make sure it stands level and stable, and that doors and drawers open and close properly where it has been placed.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Email, with the customer's signature captured on the driver's phone or tablet.** It's quicker, can't get lost, and gives both of you a record with a timestamp. Keep a few paper copies in the van for customers who prefer them or who don't use email.

## "Proof of delivery" for the part-timer

> **Proof of delivery is the record, usually a signature, photo or timestamp, showing that the item was delivered to the right person, at the right address, in the right condition.**

## Evening-before text (under 160 characters)

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Business] arrives tomorrow [time window]. We'll text when we're on the way. Questions? [Phone number]

With typical details filled in, for example:

> Hi Sarah, your furniture from Oakleaf Restoration arrives tomorrow 9-10am. We'll text when we're on the way. Questions? 01234 567890

That comes to about **132 characters**, which leaves room for longer names.

**Watch out for "smart" curly apostrophes**, which some phones and systems insert automatically, and for emojis. Either can switch the text to a different encoding that allows only 70 characters per message, so it would be sent as two or three parts. Use plain straight apostrophes (') and no emojis.
